readiness.mainReason: No blocking rule fired: the decision is clear, the recommendation is supported and gated on a soft-launch test, the framing holds and no decision-driving number is ungrounded, so only refinements remain.
readiness.highestRiskIssue: The 8% conversion assumption on slide 8 is anchored to a 32% attendance rate that measures a different behavior, though the soft launch tests it before scaling.
readiness.whatCouldChangeIt: If the named sources could not be produced, or the soft launch showed conversion well below the 5% floor, evidence quality and the recommendation's support would drop.

dimensions.name: Problem framing
dimensions.note: Specific problem (income diversification), bounded to a single-tier start, with a stated success target and no drift.

dimensions.note: Answer-first with an unbroken build, but several titles are labels so the argument is not fully readable from the titles alone.

strengths.point: The deck answers first: the recommendation is the title, so a busy reader knows the decision on slide one.
strengths.quote: Client E should launch a paid membership scheme, starting with a single tier in the autumn.

strengths.point: Key figures carry their source inline, which makes the case defensible.
strengths.quote: Project grants are 80% of Client E's income (2024 accounts) and each is single-year.

strengths.point: The plan de-risks itself with a soft-launch pilot that tests the load-bearing assumptions before scaling.
strengths.quote: A soft launch to the most engaged 200 contacts tests both before the full launch.

findings.title: The 8% conversion assumption is justified by an attendance rate that measures a different behavior.
findings.principle: Assumption discipline: a proxy metric must predict the behavior you are forecasting.
findings.diagnosis: Slide 8 calls the 8% conversion conservative against the 32% event-attendance rate. Attending an event and paying 45 pounds a year for membership are different behaviors, so attendance is a weak anchor for the conversion rate. The deck does flag the 8% as the main thing to test, which is the right instinct.

evidence.quote: The 8% assumption is conservative against the 32% attendance rate and is the main thing to test.

findings.why: If the client reads the 8% as well anchored it may under-plan for a lower result, although the soft launch limits the downside.
findings.reflect: What behavior does attendance actually predict, and is it the same behavior as paying an annual fee.
findings.fix: Separate engagement from willingness to pay. Present the soft-launch conversion as the real test of the 8% rather than leaning on the attendance rate to justify it.

findings.title: Several content-slide titles are topic labels rather than assertions.
findings.principle: Minto: the title carries the message, not the topic.
findings.diagnosis: The recommendation sits on slide 1 and the argument is easy to follow, but several content titles are bare labels. Slide 8 is titled The numbers and slide 10 is titled First steps, so a reader skimming only the titles gets the topic of each slide, not its takeaway.
findings.why: A board member who reads only the titles sees the shape of the deck but not each slide's point, so some of the argument's force is lost.
findings.reflect: If a reader saw only your titles, could they state the takeaway of each slide and not just its subject.
findings.fix: Rewrite the label titles as full-sentence assertions that state each slide's takeaway. Keep the answer-first opening you already have.

comments.problem: Month two reviews conversion against an 8% target but month three gates the full launch at 5%, and the deck does not explain the gap.
comments.why: The coordinator needs one clear decision rule for whether to go to full launch.
comments.fix: State that 5% is the floor to proceed and 8% is the year-one target, or reconcile the two numbers.

comments.problem: Comparator pricing of 40 to 60 pounds is cited but not what those groups include for it, so the 45 pound value is not benchmarked.
comments.why: The client may want to know if its benefits justify sitting near the low end of the range.
comments.fix: Add a one-line note on what the comparators offer at that price.

comments.problem: The 5,000 pounds is presented as year-one income without saying if it is gross or net of the members-only events and any costs.
comments.why: A client planning cash flow needs the net figure.
comments.fix: Label the figure gross or net.

questionsForLead: Are the named sources (2024 accounts, funder letters and comparator websites) available for a reviewer to check, since they were not attached.
Is the 5,000 pound estimate gross revenue or net of the cost of the two members-only events.
Why is the full-launch gate set at 5% when the year-one target is 8%.

learningNote.lesson: A forecast is only as good as the behavior its anchor predicts. Anchor a conversion rate to a comparable paying decision, not to a broader engagement metric.
learningNote.weakHabit: Using the metric that is on hand (attendance) as a proxy for the behavior you actually need to predict (paying for membership).
learningNote.exercise: For each assumption in a deck, write the behavior it predicts and the behavior you need, then check they match. Where they do not, name the test that would close the gap.

notAssessed: Whether the named sources (2024 accounts, funder letters and comparator websites) are accurate. They are named in the deck but were not provided.
Whether the 1,400 mailing list size and 32% attendance rate are current. Both are taken from the deck.
